item.title: [Guardian China] China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
item.description:
A man tends to a vegetable patch in the shadow of a coal-fired power station in the city of Tongling, eastern China. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
A man tends to a vegetable patch in the shadow of a coal-fired power station in the city of Tongling, eastern China. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images
China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
Decision disappoints experts hoping for world’s biggest emitter to take global lead on climate crisis
China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.
The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.
Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”
China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.
Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year. Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

item.title: [CBS News World] U.S. soldier accused of spying linked to Russia arrested in the U.K.
item.description:
A U.S. Army soldier has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia, British and U.S. authorities announced Tuesday.
The 41-year-old suspect hasn't been publicly identified, but a U.S. official told CBS News the suspect is Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
The officer was caught in a sting operation and arrested Tuesday near Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London, the official said. He is expected to be charged Sunday or Monday.
The soldier is suspected of violations under Section 1 and Section 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 — obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service, respectively. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia and that the force was carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire — the county where the base is located — related to the investigation.
The suspect was in custody in a London police station as of Tuesday, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.
"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force, said in a statement. "This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security."
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that "this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

Microsoft's popular Outlook and Teams are among the services impacted by Thursday's outage [File: Dado Ruvic/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 12 Nov 202612 Nov 2026
Thousands of Microsoft users reported trouble accessing their email and connecting to work apps after a widespread outage hit Outlook and other services on Thursday.
Reports of problems with Outlook, the company’s email client, climbed to about 130,000 on the outage tracking site Downdetector shortly after 1pm Eastern Time (18:00 GMT), with some users saying emails weren’t being sent or received, while others couldn’t open their inboxes.

By just before 3pm (20:00 GMT), that figure had fallen to about 77,000.
Users also reported having trouble accessing Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams and its AI assistant Copilot, along with other Microsoft 365 services. The company said the issues could impact users in any region.
Microsoft said on X that servers were unavailable and failing automatic health checks, putting pressure on those still operating. It said it was testing a configuration change to redistribute traffic that was elevated on parts of its infrastructure and restarting affected services to bring them back online.
“We’re working to safely return them to service,” the company said.
Microsoft did not state when it expected services to be fully restored.

item.description:

Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow was the latest of many trips the US envoys have made to see Vladimir PutinByLaura GozziPublished12 November 2026, 10:08 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held a fresh round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest discussions aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
The pair are now flying to Dublin to meet Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, and Witkoff said a new round of trilateral talks had already been agreed with Putin.
But in a sign of further tension, Zelensky said on Thursday morning that Ukraine's military was again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
The peace talks in the Emirates were framed as being centred around European security arrangements in a post-war scenario, although a resolution to the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 still appears distant.
Comments by both President Vladimir Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.
Witkoff said that Europeans would join the next round of talks. "They are our partners and it's important to us that they take part," Witkoff told Russian state TV after meeting Putin in the Kremlin.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham had said that UK national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join Zelensky, Witkoff and Kushner for talks in Dublin, but Downing Street later said they had been delayed, meaning the national security adviser could no longer join.

item.title: [NYT World] In Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner Ask Putin to Include Europe in Peace Talks
item.description:
AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.
President Trump’s envoys went to Moscow on Thursday to seek agreement from President Vladimir V. Putin to bring Europe into talks on the war in Ukraine, as the Kremlin pushes to widen the negotiations to overhaul European security arrangements.
The envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Russia one day after mediating peace talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian representatives, who spoke directly for the first time in nine months. After meeting with Mr. Putin in the Kremlin, they were scheduled to travel to Dublin to meet with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.
Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are pressing to involve Europe in the talks as Russia makes clear that it will not consider a cease-fire until its broader demands to redraw Europe’s security architecture are addressed.
The Trump administration, seeking a foreign policy win after Republicans’ drubbing in the midterm elections, is making another push for peace even as Russia gives no indication that it will stop the war anytime soon, and in fact appears to be hardening some positions.
Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of a winter bombing campaign, taking advantage of Ukraine’s lack of air defenses. On Thursday, Mr. Zelensky said that Ukraine’s armed forces again faced restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet network Starlink, and had asked U.S. officials for information.ImageA man being rescued after his apartment was struck in Kharkiv, Ukraine, last month.Credit...Mauricio Lima for The New York Times

item.title: [BBC World] Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
item.description:
Image source, Russian militaryImage caption,
The Naro-Fominsk is believed to have headed back to port in St Petersburg after the attackByPaul KirbyEurope digital editorPublished1 hour ago
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.
The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.
Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.
Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."

item.title: [CBS News World] Pope declares Peru his "homeland" in final leg of South America trip
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV declared Peru his "homeland" on Wednesday as he arrived in Lima at the start of his historic visit, returning to the place that taught him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party erupted to welcome the beloved "Padre Robert" home.
Leo seemed genuinely moved as he emerged from his charter plane, smiling broadly at nearly every turn of his first moments on Peruvian soil. The Vatican estimated that some 3 million people lined Leo's miles-long motorcade route into town, waving Peruvian and Holy See flags.
Some in the roaring crowds broke through the tight security to chase behind the car that transported him to the presidential palace, where Leo met privately with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori. During the formal welcome ceremony in the palace courtyard, he sang the Peruvian national anthem alongside Fujimori and a children's choir.
Pope Leo waves to the faithful from the popemobile on his way to Peru's government palace in Lima on Nov. 11, 2026.
Miguel Marruffo /AFP via Getty Images
In his first remarks to Fujimori and government officials, the Chicago-born Leo said the Peruvian citizenship he acquired in 2015 cemented a bond that began long before, crediting Peruvians with having formed him as a pastor by sharing their lives, joys and struggles with him.
"Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said.
"That is why I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland," he said to applause.

item.title: [BBC World] Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
item.description:
Image source, EPAImage caption,
Bomb squads have searched many schools but no devices have been foundByPaulin KolaPublished12 November 2026, 12:39 GMTUpdated 2 hours ago
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.
Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found.
The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated". Unlike a day earlier, only 77 schools were evacuated on Thursday, authorities say.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat.
Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.
The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".
Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.
A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.

Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go Nils Pratley
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability
Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.
It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.
An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.skip past newsletter promotion

Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignationByLily Jamali, North America Technology correspondent and Peter Hoskins, Business reporterPublished9 November 2026Updated 6 hours ago
One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive.
Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.
Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.
Huang admitted, external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children.
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.
Nvidia stocks plummet in US after CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy
How was Huang removed?
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company.
It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors.
But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member.
It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound".
There was no mention of the accusations of adultery.
Who will replace him?
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO.
It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis.
One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work.

item.title: [Guardian China] ‘It is much, much faster’: could China’s battery-swapping e-trucks be the answer to EV range anxiety?
item.description:
View image in fullscreen
‘It is much, much faster’: could China’s battery-swapping e-trucks be the answer to EV range anxiety?
Container trucks cross the Yanghe Bridge over Red Beach in Qingdao, Shandong, China. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Getty Images
Battery maker CATL aims to have 2,000 swapping stations in China by the end of 2027 and to bring the tech to Europe
Every day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send about five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China. A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about.
“When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts.
Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery.
In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says.
View image in fullscreen
A truck enters a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station. Photograph: CATL
Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy.

item.title: [Guardian World] Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
item.description:
‘I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey’ … Simbarashe Kundizeza
View image in fullscreen
‘I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey’ … Simbarashe Kundizeza
Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.
The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.
“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

item.title: [NYT World] A.I. Weapons Need Data for Their Training. Ukraine Has a Lot to Offer.
item.description:
AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.
The forest, seen from a drone, appeared as a vast, monotonous landscape of black tree trunks, shadows and patches of snow.
To the human eye, it appeared deserted. But to an artificial intelligence system looking for people, it did not. The system put a red box around a tiny human form, probably a soldier lurking in the trees.
Behind this feat lay vast volumes of data. Just as ChatGPT and other A.I. chatbots must be exposed to how humans write, military A.I. systems must be exposed to how humans fight. In Ukraine, this happens through a huge trove of battlefield videos, audio and text data collected over nearly five years.
The war database is being used by about 30 Ukrainian defense companies to develop A.I. weapons. Ukraine is now opening this repository, which it calls Avenger Labs, to firms in allied countries, hoping to deepen security partnerships.
Ukraine is providing the data at no charge, but companies must give the Ukrainian military licenses to any software they develop. Under the first agreement to be reached, 12 British defense companies will gain access. Ukraine is in talks with other countries.
While there is no shortage of Western companies developing autonomous weapons, there is a shortage of the data needed to train them. Ukraine can offer more of it than any other potential partner.

item.title: [ABC News World] This Beirut family has sold falafel for 100 years, through war and crisis. It has no plan to stop
item.description:
This Beirut family has sold falafel for 100 years, through war and crisis. It has no plan to stop
The Tabbara family has been making falafel in Lebanon for over a centuryByBASSEM MROUE Associated PressNovember 12, 2026, 12:27 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BEIRUT -- For more than a century, the Tabbara family has been serving up falafel to Beirut’s residents.
Their business, which predates Lebanon’s founding, has survived two world wars and a series of local conflicts in the small Mediterranean nation.
Now, a fourth generation is getting ready to take over the modest shop, where customers can get $3 sandwiches of small, doughnut-shaped patties of deep-fried ground fava beans wrapped in flat Lebanese bread with pickled cucumber, tomatoes, parsley, thick tahini sauce and homemade dark red-hot pepper paste for the spice lovers.
“I have clients spread all over the world,” 82-year-old Mohammed Tabbara said as a European customer waited for a sandwich in Beirut’s busy Hamra district that's packed with cafes, clothing shops and two major universities.
“They all come to eat falafel because they know the flavor and the taste,” Tabbara added.
He is passing down the culinary craft to his 40-year-old son, Ziad Tabbara, a former accountant who has spent the last six years working full time with his dad.
“This is a flavor that made history and heritage passed down through generations,” said Ziad Tabbara, who as a child helped his father in the shop during summer vacations.
Ziad has no children of his own to pass on the tradition to — a sore point with his father who wants to see him married with children.
Beirut was still part of the Ottoman Empire when Ziad's great-grandfather Kamel Tabbara opened the family’s first falafel shop in the city’s central Bab Idriss district in 1914. It would be six years before the state of Greater Lebanon was established after World War I.

A Mexican Singer Gives Old Ballads New Heroines
Grammy-nominated songwriter Vivir Quintana is known throughout Latin America for giving voice to women who fought back against domestic violence.
Vivir Quintana in Oaxaca.Credit...
Supported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENT

By Paulina Villegas
Photographs by Victoria Razo
Reporting from Oaxaca, MexicoNov. 12, 2026Leer en español
Against the backdrop of a centuries-old stone church in the Mexican city of Oaxaca, the singer Vivir Quintana raised her deep, husky voice above the blare of trumpets, trombones and the booming pulse of a tuba.
Behind her stood a brass band of young Indigenous girls in embroidered white blouses and brightly colored skirts. Hat in hand and fist raised, Ms. Quintana sang a corrido, a traditional Mexican folk ballad usually used to recount tales of revolutionaries, outlaws, folk heroes, and more recently, drug traffickers.
Corridos are typically sung by men, about men. Ms. Quintana sang a corrido she wrote based on the true story of a woman who fought back when her abusive partner tried to gouge out her eyes with a knife.
“I used to think that what united us women was our pain. Now I have realized it is love and resistance,” Ms. Quintana told the crowd in October during a women’s conference in Oaxaca called Decididas, drawing a roar of applause. “We must keep defending ourselves!”
On Thursday, Ms. Quintana will take the stage at the Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas alongside the Colombian pop superstar Juanes, with whom she is nominated for song of the year for “Humano.” It is her second Latin Grammy nomination.Image

item.title: [ABC News World] Brazil fines Facebook $1.3M for failing to comply with court orders during election
item.description:
Brazil fines Facebook $1.3M for failing to comply with court orders during election
Brazil’s top electoral court fines Meta’s Facebook $1.3 million for not fully complying with judicial orders during the recent presidential election runoff campaignByELÉONORE HUGHES Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 12:23 PM
Share
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazil’s top electoral court fined Meta’s Facebook $1.3 million for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month’s presidential election runoff campaign when the company was accused of political bias by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ’s team.
Justices ruled late Tuesday that Facebook had failed to adequately meet court demands related to allegations that its platform treated content from Lula and challenger Flávio Bolsonaro differently but said there was no evidence so far that the company attempted to influence the election’s outcome.
“Such a conclusion would require compelling evidence of intent, to be presented in full proceedings through the appropriate legal channels,” Justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze said in his decision that was unanimously accepted by his colleagues.
Ahead of the runoff vote, Lula’s campaign filed a lawsuit claiming that the company owning Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp was using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favor Bolsonaro.
The accusation gained traction among Lula's supporters and sparked a protest in front of Meta's offices in Sao Paulo.
Meta said in response that a series of recent platform issues stemmed from unrelated global technical glitches, strict anti-fraud measures and regulatory compliance rather than targeted suppression. The tech giant also told the court that it had adopted measures to ensure equal treatment of the two campaigns.
But Bellizze said that while the company had submitted statements and documents regarding the measures, some court orders were not followed or were fulfilled incompletely or late.

item.title: [ABC News World] Islamic State group-affiliated rebels kill at least 22 in Congo's eastern region
item.description:
Islamic State group-affiliated rebels kill at least 22 in Congo's eastern region
A rebel group affiliated with the Islamic State group has killed at least 22 people in Congo's eastern Ituri provinceByJEAN-YVES KAMALE Associated Press and JUSTIN KABUMBA Associated PressNovember 11, 2026, 11:52 AM
Share
ITURI, Congo -- At least 22 people were killed in a series of attacks by a rebel group affiliated with the Islamic State group between Tuesday and Wednesday in Congo 's eastern Ituri province.
The attacks were carried out by the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) across eight locations in the Mambasa territory in Ituri, according to two civil society and human rights monitoring groups.
At least 10 people were also abducted.
“The death toll remains provisional. In addition to the 22 civilians killed, the perpetrators abducted other individuals, and motorcycles and homes were set on fire,” said Marie-Noelle Anatobe, coordinator of the Civil Society of Congo in Mambasa territory.
The attacks happened in nearly inaccessible locations near the border between Uganda and Congo.
The ADF grew out of Uganda and was pushed to the border region with Congo, where it has operated for years, targeting civilians. It pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group in 2019.
Both the Ugandan and Congolese armies have been jointly attacking the group, but they have long struggled against it.

item.description:

Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested himByJoe Pike, politics investigations correspondent and Phil Kemp, politics reporterPublished11 November 2026
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".
Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.
The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.
Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.
The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.
Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.
In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.
But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.
Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.

item.title: [BBC China] Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boomByKali Hays, Technology reporter and Lily Jamali, North America Technology correspondentPublished10 November 2026
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe.
The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.
Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools.
It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race.
Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.
Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.
Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.

Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.
A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

item.title: [Guardian World] Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
item.description:
People at the scene of the collision in Giza province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
People at the scene of the collision in Giza province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.
An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.
The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.
Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.
Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.
Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.
View image in fullscreen
People search for survivors after the collision. Photograph: AP
Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.
